messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prison Guard
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 42

Marcelo, a 28-year-old Latin American man, works as a prison guard. His life took an unexpected and tragic turn when he lost his younger brother, Juan, in a car accident two years ago. Since that day, Marcelo has found himself struggling with intrusive thoughts about the accident and feelings of intense grief and helplessness. Marcelo describes waking up each morning to the same recurring nightmare: he sees Juan's car spinning out of control on the rain-soaked highway, unable to regain traction or stop. Each time he wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart pounding as if it might jump out of his chest. The vividness of these nightmares has made sleep a precarious and frightening experience for Marcelo. At work, Marcelo's concentration is often compromised by the intrusive thoughts that keep him tethered to Juan’s death. He frequently finds himself zoning out during routine tasks, only to snap back to reality with an alarming start. His colleagues have noticed his distraction but haven't pressed him about it, perhaps sensing the discomfort of the topic. Recently, Marcelo has become increasingly avoidant. He avoids listening to music they used to enjoy together and even hesitates to drive on roads he associates with Juan’s accident route. When he does drive, he feels a constant sense of anxiety and hypervigilance, always scanning for any potential danger that might remind him of what happened. Marcelo's marriage has also been affected by his struggles. His wife, Sofia, senses the distance between them but isn't sure how to bridge it. Marcelo often withdraws into himself after work, spending long hours alone in their apartment, staring at the walls or pacing back and forth. He’s reluctant to engage with family gatherings that might bring up memories of Juan, which has led to some tension within his close-knit community. One day, as he's patrolling the prison compound, Marcelo hears a car engine revving outside the gates—a sound eerily reminiscent of the moment before Juan’s crash. His heart races, and he experiences a sudden surge of panic. He feels dizzy and disoriented, needing to pause momentarily to regain his composure before continuing with his duties. Despite these challenges, Marcelo tries to maintain a semblance of normalcy. He remains committed to his work as a prison guard because it provides him with a sense of structure and purpose that helps ground him in the present moment. Yet, even this grounding can be disrupted by sudden waves of grief that hit without warning, especially when he encounters inmates who remind him of Juan’s age or personality. Marcelo finds himself questioning how to move forward, feeling stuck between his past and a future without his brother. He often wonders if these feelings will ever subside or if they are an inevitable part of his new reality. Despite the overwhelming emotions that continue to plague him, he holds onto hope that one day, perhaps with time, he might find a way to integrate these memories into his life in a more manageable way. In his moments of clarity, Marcelo reflects on how resilient Juan was and hopes to embody that strength. He knows it's not an easy journey but feels compelled to keep going for the sake of both himself and those around him who love and support him deeply.
